site.name: Xinyu Wang
site.intro: Structures that respond to people and time: canopies that open for a market, rooms that step down a hillside, a projected doorway that wakes as you approach.

about.headline: Xinyu Wang is an architecture student working between structure, material and public life.
bio: A senior in the BFA Architectural Design program at Parsons School of Design in New York (b. 2004).

Xinyu's projects start from a specific place and a specific time of day, and test ideas through models, drawings and simple simulations: where the sun falls at four in the afternoon, how a cart folds, how light reaches a corridor three floors down.

The projects here range from studio buildings to an interactive installation, a speculative city and an urban plan for Porto. Read together, they are a record of learning to build with light, structure and public life.

site.work_note: Studio buildings, an interactive installation, a speculative city and an urban plan for Porto.

projects.title: Osborn Plaza Market Canopy
projects.summary: A fleet of deployable bamboo-and-reed carts that turns a Brownsville plaza into a Wednesday farmers' market, then folds down into everyday shaded seating.
lede: Osborn Plaza sits on a raised block of the former Osborn Street. It has trees, murals and movable cafe tables, but little shade in the late afternoon, exactly when a neighbourhood market would open.

The project proposes one deployable unit that works in three modes. On market day 15 units line a single aisle from the south gate to Belmont Avenue; the rest of the week 10 of them drop to bench height and give the plaza shaded seats. Bamboo carries, reed shades, planting cools.

text: Peak summer, June to August, noon to 5 pm, simulated with Ladybug Tools and Radiance on the site model and a LiDAR model of the neighbouring buildings. The market canopies cut solar radiation on the plaza by 21% and on the ground beneath them by two thirds; the everyday benches cut it by 13%.

On a 92 °F July afternoon the whole plaza is in strong heat stress, with or without canopies, but very strong heat stress (UTCI above 38 °C) drops from 21% to 9% of the plaza. The reed lets 30% of the sun through, trading a little shade for airflow.

items.caption: Cumulative solar radiation, June-August 12:00-17:00 (no canopies / market day / everyday), and UTCI at 14:00 on a July heat day.
Sun angle test, 21 July: 65-68% of the plaza is in direct sun at 13:00-14:00; the market canopies bring this down to 52-54%.

text: A hybrid frame keeps 5 aluminium spine rails that carry the lift mechanism and replaces the wings with laminated bamboo, cutting frame emissions by about half while storing carbon.

Planted boxes at both ends bring back the green, cooling edge of the first study. Every joint is bolted, pinned or clipped, so worn parts are swapped rather than repaired; bamboo rails sit on the mast heads through stainless knife plates and isolated bolts.

items.caption: One unit taken apart, drawn from the model: reed shade panels, bamboo wings, aluminium masts, table slats, lift and chassis, with the two planted boxes slid out.

The joint between bamboo and metal, 3" = 1'-0": a steel knife plate slots into the laminated bamboo rail and two stainless bolts pin it to the mast head; rubber and nylon keep the bamboo off the metal.
Market day with the planted boxes at the ends of each cart.

text: Food, health, heat, mobility, housing and water around the plaza, read at four scales: the city, Community District 16, the five-minute walk and the plaza itself. Every map is drawn from NYC open data at a true scale.

Grocery stores are within 300 ft, yet premature death is twice the city rate; heat vulnerability is 5 of 5; seven in ten households have no car; 83% of homes within a five-minute walk are NYCHA. The canopy is a walking market and daily shade for its neighbours, not more retail.

projects.title: The Vertical Village
projects.place: Washington Ave, Clinton Hill, Brooklyn, NY
projects.summary: Affordable housing stacked above a public library. A glass-and-timber core joins the reading floors, and walkable glass plates in the corridors pull daylight down through the homes.
lede: Clinton Hill grew from Dutch farmland into the "Gold Coast" mansions of Clinton Avenue, then was subdivided into rooming houses when the Navy Yard brought wartime workers. The project adds to that layered density: a public library on the ground and cellar floors, with three floors of affordable homes above.

Two strategies organise it. In the library, a glazed accessible elevator wrapped by a U-shaped wooden reading stair turns circulation into a gathering landscape. On the residential floors, staggered "Tetris" glass plates set into the corridor slabs act as light wells, so the double-loaded corridor becomes a bright interior street.

projects.title: Between Levels
projects.summary: A common street across three levels: a hillside neighbourhood building where a shared stair-street, galleries and 48 public rooms connect streets 12 m apart.
lede: Three streets enter a sloping site at +0, +6 and +12 m. Instead of one building per street, two stepped wings on a 36 x 48 m grid share a continuous stair-street and covered galleries, so the building works as a public route as much as a container.
12 room types, from a repair shop to a reading lounge, are deployed as 48 rooms across 5 floors. Each was furnished for its actual width rather than copied and renamed.

projects.title: Threshold Apparatus
projects.tools: Arduino Uno, ultrasonic sensor, Processing, projector
projects.summary: An interactive moving-image study of bodily proximity: a sensor reads how close you are to a doorway, and a projected mesh wakes, deforms and settles as you approach, pause and pass.
lede: Everyday life is full of moments between entering and not yet entering: a pause at a doorway, a slower step at a corridor corner, a moment of hesitation before a glass door. They suggest that a spatial boundary is not only a static element, but something perceived and activated by the body's approach, pause and passage.

The project asks how interactive moving image can make that threshold visible. Projected onto real transitional spaces, the image stops being something to look at and becomes part of the boundary itself: a spatial skin that responds to the body.

stats.label: bodily actions mapped: approach, pause, proximity, crossing, occupying

items.hint: Scroll to walk up to the door, drag to turn it
items.caption: The installation rebuilt as a live diagram: a visitor walks toward a doorway, the ultrasonic sensor above it reads the distance, and the triangulated skin projected on the wall wakes, peaks at the threshold and settles after they pass.

text: In architecture, a threshold is not simply a doorway or an edge but a transitional condition, connecting inside and outside, open and closed, public and private. Its meaning lies less in form than in how it organises action and perception.

As one approaches a doorway, the body slows; before a transparent boundary, one checks whether entry is possible; in a narrow passage, posture adjusts. Space is not passively used but continuously formed through its relationship with the body.

items.caption: Body-threshold-space relation matrix: approach, pause, proximity, crossing and occupying, read as movement, threshold state, perception and spatial response.

text: So the project should not simply be an interactive video. Moving image acts as a visual skin; bodily distance, movement, pause and orientation are the perceptual data; the image is a threshold field that deforms, expands or contracts; and the physical space is the framework in which meaning is made.

items.caption: The logic of responsive spatial generation, in four layers: visual skin, perceptual data, threshold field and spatial framework.

text: An Arduino reads distance in real time through an ultrasonic sensor and sends it to Processing over serial. Processing maps the distance to an interaction value that drives mesh displacement, colour, opacity and interference.
The value is smoothed, so the image responds gradually rather than switching on and off: the threshold reads as a continuous spatial event.

items.caption: Interaction flow, State 0 to State 4: idle range, detection, mid-range response, peak threshold and residual closure.

items.hint: Scroll through the five captured states
items.caption: The five states as captured from the Processing sketch: still while no one is near, waking as a body enters the sensor's range, peaking at the threshold and settling into a residual trace after they leave.

projects.title: Above the Waterline
projects.summary: A vertical city for a time of rising seas: abandoned high-rises become the foundations for new settlement, grown upward in Unreal Engine 5 by procedural rules.
lede: As rising seas reduce habitable land, the project imagines existing high-rise buildings as the foundation for new forms of settlement. Through adaptive reuse, modular expansion and ecological integration, a vertical urban ecosystem grows upward.

It was developed in Unreal Engine 5 with Procedural Content Generation: rule-based systems generate architectural modules, parasitic structures, vegetation and spatial hierarchies, simulating how a vertical city attaches, expands and evolves.

text: Floating villages in Southeast Asia and post-disaster housing show how modular expansion, self-organised growth and shared infrastructure let communities function with limited resources. Their growth follows a process of attachment, expansion, accumulation and evolution.
In a vertical city, limited space does not remove inequality but amplifies it: resources, energy and living conditions are stratified by elevation, from a flooded foundation to a sky garden district.

text: A modular building library divides architecture into facade, floor, roof and base units that can be reassembled by rule. PCG graphs then generate the city from adjustable parameters: building height, density, attachment distance, growth direction and randomness.

projects.title: Human Race Motor
projects.summary: A city grown by rules instead of drawn by hand: cellular automata generate unit towers, the best are selected as the shell, and a space city takes shape around four zones and walkways in zero gravity.
lede: Technology and nature are two routes through the long river of human civilisation, each moving forward on its own track until they meet at the far end. The history of technology is a process of constantly stealing fire; where people gather, everyday city life becomes its most authentic exhibition.

Here the city is generated rather than drawn. Cellular automata, which can simulate how complex systems evolve in space and time, grow a field of unit towers. Selected by set rules, the towers become the outer shell that houses the city's functional blocks, organised into four zones and threaded by walkways.

text: The research sets the space race beside a century of urban models, from the City Beautiful and the Garden City to the sustainable city.

Four cities show how blocks change over time: in Melbourne plots consolidate from the economic centre out to the fringe; in Barcelona blocks group into communities and then urban areas; Paris opens wide channels so the city can breathe; Manhattan grows vertically, up and into the basement.

text: The city is divided into four zones: government offices, law enforcement and science labs; housing, a hospital and shopping; transport; and manufacturing.

text: In a society that only focuses on work and production, housing grows layer by layer around the workplace and takes over every open space. Yet people always find the space that has not been built on yet and make it a place to meet; when it is built over, they find new space.

Without gravity, people can move between buildings and districts at will, while the city keeps fixed lines of transport. The walkways above the transport pipes are among the few places left for people to walk and talk.

projects.title: Triangle Commons
projects.place: New York Botanical Garden, Bronx, NY
projects.summary: A multi-purpose building for the New York Botanical Garden: triangular pavilions on slender columns, rotated off one triangular grid, stepping down a slope to the water and bridging the road beside it.
lede: On a slope in the New York Botanical Garden in the Bronx, between a road and the water, the site is first filled as a solid, then cut by a triangular grid. Triangles are aligned to the grid, duplicated and rotated, and the leftover gaps become a continuous route: up from the road, over a bridge, through the decks and down to the water.

Enclosed triangles hold a library, workspaces and a cafe deck with planted roofs. Between them, perforated dark canopies on a forest of thin white columns shade an open plaza, where the light changes from morning to afternoon.

projects.title: From Urbanity to Nature
projects.summary: A wine culture community on the last unbuilt stretch of Porto's Douro riverfront: vineyards, orchards, a winery, homes and a hotel woven into the park, so the journey to port wine ends inside the city.
lede: Porto has been transformed over the last decade, and the Douro riverfront has drawn the most building. Aleixo, a social housing complex under demolition, is the last front of the river without construction: a green valley with a natural cliff dropping to the river and the sea. Should we build there, and how can nature and architecture be balanced?

Visitors come to Porto for its wine, yet the vineyards and wineries are far from the centre. The project keeps the green texture of the land but turns it into urban agriculture, and adds a winery, homes, a trade centre and a hotel, so that wine tourists and locals meet in one community: production and consumption, nature and architecture, making and enjoying.

text: Porto is one of the most popular cities in Europe and famous for its wine, but the vineyards and wineries visitors want to see are far from the centre.

Three things make Aleixo the site: a green park with abandoned buildings and a natural cliff over the river and the sea; the last unbuilt front on the Douro; and the tourist tram that passes through it. The Douro, the river of wine, is drawn in red.

text: The site was a green area with two walls. The structure preserves the landscape and opens to the city from every corner. Organic and strong paths merge into one journey that ends at the pier or at the green amphitheatre of the park.
Visitors can walk over the buildings, through the landscape, or from one to the other, as the ground gradually sinks; the path offers the landscape to every sense.

text: The journey is designed around five senses. Smell: the aromas of grapes, fruit and vegetables through the year. Touch: the ups and downs of the landscape and the textured walls on the way to the winery. Sight: from the top of the winery, a panoramic view of the Douro and the pier.
Taste: wine and local cuisine with the best views. Hearing: wind through the trees, and water running from the highest point along the winery down to the pond in the park.

projects.title: Transforming Light
projects.summary: How can architectural screens make changes in sunlight visible through patterns of light and shadow? A study of ten screens from Ahmedabad to Abu Dhabi.
lede: A short research presentation on how buildings help us notice natural change and the passage of time. Each precedent is read through one variable: opening, scale, angle, surface, depth, movement or panel position.
The study ends with a test method for the studio: keep the screen fixed and move the lamp; keep the lamp fixed and change one screen variable at a time.
projects.note: Precedent photographs are from the course image archive and are shown for academic research; credit belongs to the original photographers.
